title: Two lines into the body: vagal and spinal
objective: Contrast vagal (nodose) and spinal (DRG) visceral afferents by route and territory.

steps.title: Nodose vs DRG
steps.body:
The viscera are watched by two afferent systems:

- **Vagal** afferents — cell bodies in the **[[nodose ganglion]]** — run in the **[[vagus]]** to the brainstem; densest in the **upper** GI tract (stomach, duodenum).
- **Spinal** afferents — cell bodies in the **[[DRG]]** — run to the spinal cord; spread **throughout**, densest **distally** (the [[colon]]).

steps.prompt: Match each visceral afferent system to its features.
pairs: To the brainstem; densest in the upper gut
To the spinal cord; densest in the distal gut
steps.explanation: Vagal afferents report to the brainstem and dominate the proximal gut; spinal/DRG afferents report to the cord and dominate distally.

steps.setup: You record from an afferent innervating the distal colon and trace its cell body.
steps.prompt: Where do you most likely find that cell body?
options: The dorsal horn of the cord
steps.reveal: The distal colon is dominated by spinal afferents, whose cell bodies sit in the DRG (vagal/nodose coverage thins out distally). The dorsal horn is where their central branch synapses, not where the cell body lives.

variants.prompt: A distal-colon afferent's cell body is most likely in…
variants.explanation: Spinal/DRG afferents dominate the distal colon; nodose coverage is proximal.

steps.title: Why the split matters
steps.body: Routing differs, so the two systems feed different circuits and are studied with different tools. For the lab, the spinal/DRG line into the distal gut — and, by extension, other organs like the pancreas — is the one under the microscope.

sources.note: Spinal (DRG) vs vagal innervation of the gut; the DRG side is the frontier.

reviewNotes: Vagal vs spinal visceral afferents; nodose vs DRG.
